plan.topic: Thanksgiving dinner on tirzepatide: why you may feel full fast at a big meal (slower gastric emptying, label wording) and calm ways to make the day easier
plan.angle:
08:00 body-worry Short, 60–85 s, 170 words or fewer.

Answer within 10 s: 'Will Thanksgiving dinner make you sick on tirzepatide? Not necessarily, but a big, rich meal may sit heavier, because tirzepatide can slow how fast food leaves your stomach' (label wording).

The new fact is the label's gastric-emptying wording plus the common GI side effects it lists. Then our own untagged tips:
- start with a small plate built around turkey or another protein you enjoy
- eat slowly
- stop at comfortably full
- sip fluids unless you've been told to limit them

Alcohol: make no sourced claim; just say ask your prescriber. People who also use insulin or a sulfonylurea should ask their prescriber about the holiday meal (label: higher low-blood-sugar risk).

Red flag, in label wording: severe stomach pain that won't go away means contact your healthcare provider.

Also required:
- 'Don't skip, move or change your injection or dose around the holiday on your own.'
- No guilt, no foods labelled 'bad', no calorie talk.
- Exp F line second to last, then 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line, both spoken and on screen.
- Last line: 'Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description.' The publisher puts the Thanksgiving long video's link on description line 1.

Mix at masking 0.02 or lower.

package.title: Thanksgiving on Tirzepatide: Will You Feel Sick? #shorts
package.description:
Feeling full fast on tirzepatide isn't failure. The label says tirzepatide delays gastric emptying, so food can leave your stomach more slowly. Its most common side effects include nausea, diarrhea, vomiting and indigestion.
On insulin or a sulfonylurea? The label notes a higher risk of low blood sugar, so ask your prescriber about the holiday meal. Don't skip, move or change your injection or dose around the holiday on your own. Severe stomach pain that won't go away? Contact your healthcare provider right away.
Sources: Zepbound (tirzepatide) Prescribing Information, revised 8/2026: https://uspl.lilly.com/zepbound/zepbound.html#pi | Mounjaro (tirzepatide) Prescribing Information, revised 8/2026: https://uspl.lilly.com/mounjaro/mounjaro.html#pi
#Tirzepatide #Zepbound #Mounjaro #GLP1 #Thanksgiving
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
I checked every label claim against the current Zepbound and Mounjaro prescribing information. Both are on uspl.lilly.com and both say "Revised: 8/2026".

- **Slower stomach emptying (s2):** both labels say it word for word ("ZEPBOUND/MOUNJARO delays gastric emptying"), so the quoted fragment is accurate.
- **Common side effects (s3):** nausea, vomiting and dyspepsia (indigestion) are on both labels' most-common lists (≥5%). The word "include" makes the partial list accurate.
- **Low blood sugar (s5):** the Mounjaro label says insulin or a sulfonylurea "may have an increased risk of hypoglycemia, including severe hypoglycemia". The Zepbound label reports 10.3% vs 2.1% with sulfonylureas in people with diabetes.
- **When to get help (s7):** "severe stomach pain that won't go away" matches the labels' pancreatitis warning. Leaving out the label's "stop using" fits brand rules, and "contact your healthcare provider right away" is safe.
- **Tips (s4):** these are our own general tips and are correctly left without a source. The fluids caveat and the "ask your prescriber about alcohol" line are there.
- **Safety lines:** the don't-change-your-dose line, the disclaimer and the prescriber line are all spoken and shown on screen.
- **Length:** narration is about 167 words, under the 170 limit.
- **Title:** it's answered honestly ("Not necessarily") and doesn't scare.

There are no factual or safety errors. The listed fixes are minor wording changes for the muted-viewer test and fuller label wording.

issues.problem: A muted viewer sees a worry question with no drug named and no calm answer. The narration answers 'Not necessarily' straight away, so the text tells less than the voice does and reads as scarier.

issues.claim: Tirzepatide's most common side effects include nausea, vomiting and indigestion.
issues.problem: This is accurate because it says 'include'. But diarrhea is the second most common side effect on both labels and is missing, which matters for a heavy holiday meal.
issues.fix: Narration: "Tirzepatide's most common side effects include nausea, diarrhea, vomiting and indigestion." On-screen: "Common: nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, indigestion". Add 'Diarrhea' as item 2 in the list visual. This adds 1 word, about 168 in total.

issues.problem: The on-screen text leaves out the reason the narration gives (higher risk of low blood sugar), so a muted viewer doesn't learn why.
issues.fix: Insulin or sulfonylurea? Low blood sugar risk: ask prescriber

issues.problem: It drops 'stomach' and 'right away', both in the narration and the label wording, so the red flag is broader and less urgent than the voice.

issues.problem: It's acceptable as written. The on-screen text only mentions doses, while the narration also covers skipping and moving the injection.
